children: City Therapeutics, a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing RNA interference (RNAi) medicines, filed an S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq Global Market under the ticker CTY. The IPO is led by Goldman Sachs, Jefferies, Stifel and Oppenheimer. Proceeds will fund clinical trials for its lead programs in thrombosis, Stargardt disease and anemia of chronic disease, and further platform development.

City Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing next‑generation RNA interference (RNAi) medicines aimed at silencing disease‑relevant proteins. Its lead program, CITY‑FXI, is a GalNAc‑conjugated siRNA targeting Factor XI to prevent pathological thrombosis with the goal of reducing bleeding risk relative to current anticoagulants; Phase 1 data in healthy volunteers showed dose‑dependent FXI knockdown, and a Phase 2 study in total knee arthroplasty is planned. CITY‑RBP4 targets retinol binding protein 4 to reduce toxic vitamin A byproducts in Stargardt disease, with a Phase 1 start planned in late 2026 and potential expansion into Geographic Atrophy. CITY‑TFR2 targets transferrin receptor 2 to lower hepcidin and restore iron availability for anemia of chronic disease, beginning with myelofibrosis‑associated anemia via an investigator‑initiated trial in China in late 2026 and a company‑sponsored Phase 1/2 in early 2027.

The company’s City Platform integrates RNAi trigger engineering (including proprietary cityRNA triggers), novel tissue‑targeted delivery ligands (e.g., LRP1 for ocular/CNS), and AI/ML‑enabled design to identify potent, specific, and durable RNAi candidates. Strategic collaborations with Bausch + Lomb (retinal diseases) and Biogen (CNS neurodegenerative diseases) complement City’s wholly owned pipeline while preserving core platform rights.
: Anticoagulants market estimated at ~$37 billion in 2025, projected to reach ~$56 billion by 2033.
: RNAi field expanding with ~100 clinical programs and eight FDA-approved RNAi medicines since 2018.
: Pipeline targets large unmet needs in thromboembolic disease, inherited retinal disease, and anemia of chronic disease with genetics-led RNAi candidates.

: Alnylam, Ionis, Arrowhead, Novartis, Lilly, GSK, AstraZeneca, Silence Therapeutics, Novo Nordisk, ADARx, Sarepta, Sirius; FXI competitors include Bayer, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Johnson & Johnson, Regeneron; Stargardt competitors include Alkeus and Belite Bio; anemia competitors include Disc Medicine and ESA/HIF-PH approaches.
: Next-generation trigger engineering and extrahepatic delivery (e.g., ocular/CNS) are extending RNAi’s reach beyond liver targets.
: Headquarters and labs in Cambridge, Massachusetts (51,726 sq. ft.)
: United States; planned IIT in China
: Bausch + Lomb (ocular RNAi program); Biogen (systemic CNS RNAi program)
: Increased from $2.8 million in 2024 to $13.6 million in 2025
, President and Chief Executive Officer - Former senior executive at Alnylam and Chief Commercial Officer at Krystal Biotech; 25+ years in developing and launching novel medicines.
, Executive Chair - Founding CEO of Alnylam; led development and approval of the first wave of FDA‑approved RNAi therapeutics.
, Chief Financial Officer - Former CFO of Keros Therapeutics and Wave Life Sciences; finance leadership roles at Shire and Biogen.
, Chief Medical Officer - Former CMO at Editas; led development of multiple approved biologics and an siRNA medicine at Sanofi and Biogen.
, Chief Scientific Officer - RNAi pioneer; leadership roles at Alnylam and Generation Bio; co‑inventor/contributor to several approved RNAi medicines.
, Chief Operating Officer - Co‑founder; company creation and operating roles at RTW Investments and Flagship Pioneering.
: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC; Jefferies; Stifel; Oppenheimer & Co.

: Fund CITY-FXI through Phase 1 and initiate a Phase 2 TKA study; advance CITY-RBP4 through Phase 1 and preparations for Stargardt disease and Geographic Atrophy; advance CITY-TFR2 through an IIT in China and a Phase 1/2 trial; continue platform and discovery programs; working capital and general purposes.
